idiom_name: companion object apply / named factory methods (constructor proxies, case-class apply)
implementation_notes: Scala pushes this pattern into the language: an apply in the companion object makes Person("Fred") compile without new, case classes get that apply generated for free, and Scala 3 emits constructor proxies for plain classes, so ordinary call syntax already routes through a factory the definition can override. Named routes for different construction intents go beside apply (fromJson, List.fill, BigDecimal(...)), and the companion object returns a base type or interface to hide implementations exactly as the collection companions do. The classic private-constructor-plus-static-methods structure is absorbed by the companion object; make the primary constructor private only when validation must be unavoidable, because apply is sugar, not a guarantee.
code_sketch:
final class Email private (val value: String)
object Email:
  def apply(text: String): Email =            // override the construction sugar
    val v = text.trim.toLowerCase
    require(v.contains("@"), "invalid address")
    new Email(v)
  def fromUserId(id: Long): Email = Email(s"user$id@example.com")

// val e = Email("A@B.io")   -> Email.apply("A@B.io")
pitfalls: apply is sugar over a normal method: Email(...) may validate, cache or return a subtype, and callers cannot see which - document the behaviour because the call looks like a constructor.
A case class generates its own apply, copy and unapply, so adding a validating apply leaves copy able to bypass validation; use a plain class with a companion apply when invariants must hold.

Companion-object state (caches, counters) is effectively global and lazily initialized per classloader; thread safety and initialization order of a cached instance are the implementer's responsibility.
